world: W WRITTEN-IN -- recoverable only from post-exposure text
outcome_variable_scope: The label is sign(mean score) over a criterion's released ratings -- a HUMAN quantity, not a model gold head. No judge and no response text enters this round at any point.
scope: Prompts are held out entirely (GroupKFold on prompt id), so no criterion from a test prompt informs training. This does NOT measure whether any person held a direction before seeing the menu -- that is S_pre and it remains unreachable in this release. It measures whether the direction is a function of the criterion's semantics. A shared phrasing convention is a live alternative and its control is reported.
verdict: W WRITTEN-IN -- recoverable only from post-exposure text. THE PROVENANCE SPLIT INVERTS THE NAIVE READING, and it is the whole result. Criteria whose TEXT is response-blind -- the pre-written seed class, shown to every rater before they wrote anything -- carry essentially NO text-recoverable direction beyond their marginal: +0.0020 [-0.0007,+0.0049], which is 1.2% of the headroom available to them. Criteria composed AFTER the annotator read all four responses carry +0.0821 [+0.0746,+0.0904], or 26.4% of theirs. Normalising by headroom is required here and not cosmetic: the seed marginal is 0.8400 against 0.6886, so the arms had very different room to gain and the raw margins are not comparable. SO THE DIRECTION IS RECOVERABLE FROM WORDING PRECISELY WHERE THE WORDING WAS COMPOSED WITH THE MENU IN VIEW. That is the signature of construction, not of a prior: a rater who has seen the responses writes the direction into the sentence. It is not evidence that a pre-menu direction is absent -- nothing here can see one -- but it removes the reading that text-predictability demonstrates one. The README's R-layer row says a response-blind direction is unreachable because no rater in the release rated a criterion before seeing four responses. That is exactly right about what it says, and this round neither contradicts nor measures it. It measures a different quantity the release does contain: whether the direction is recoverable from the criterion's WORDS, with no response entering the computation at any point. Predicting sign(mean score) from text alone with prompts held out entirely, over 15223 criteria on 986 prompts: accuracy 0.7868 against a majority-class marginal of 0.7435, i.e. +0.0434 above it [+0.0385,+0.0480] under a prompt-clustered bootstrap. Controls ran first and both are required to pass: shuffling labels inside training collapses to 0.7429 (-0.0006 above marginal), and the in-sample fit reaches 0.8516, so a held-out null would have been a measurement rather than silence. BY PROVENANCE: the seed class -- pre-written and shown to every rater -- scores +0.0020 above its marginal, and write-ins, composed with the menu in view, +0.0821. THE CONFOUND, WRITTEN BEFORE THE RUN: a shared phrasing convention would produce this without anyone holding a prior direction, since 'avoid X' carries its sign in its grammar. Restricted to criteria with no overt negation marker the margin is +0.0499 on 11423 items, so the grammatical shortcut does not account for it. WHAT THIS CHANGES: S_pre's human arm is preregistered against r61's chance baseline of 0.6459, which is the RATING marginal. For the PRE arm the relevant baseline is now sharper still -- a text-only predictor scores 0.8420 on exactly the class of criteria an S_pre participant would face (pre-written, response-blind), which is +0.0020 above the marginal and therefore adds nothing beyond it. So for SEEDS the preregistered baseline needs no adjustment, and that is a positive result for the design. Where it does need adjusting is any arm using WRITE-IN text, where a text-only predictor already captures 26.4% of the headroom and a human PRE arm could score well while measuring the phrasing convention twice.
